summary: Dapsone is a sulfone with antimycobacterial and anti-inflammatory (PMN-modulating) activity. It is the mainstay sulfone for dermatitis herpetiformis and a key component of multidrug therapy for leprosy, and is also used for Pneumocystis prophylaxis/treatment. Major hazards are dose-related hemolysis (severe in G6PD deficiency), methemoglobinemia, agranulocytosis/aplastic anemia, and the dapsone hypersensitivity (DRESS) syndrome.
indications: Leprosy (all forms except proven dapsone resistance), in combination with other anti-leprosy drugs
(Off-label/established) Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis and treatment in sulfa-intolerant patients

dosage.d: Start 50 mg daily; titrate within 50-300 mg/day; higher if needed
dosage.n: Reduce to lowest maintenance dose once controlled
A gluten-free diet may allow dose reduction/elimination

dosage.d: 100 mg daily without interruption, with one or more other anti-leprosy drugs
dosage.n: Continued per WHO multidrug regimen duration
Per body weight and WHO regimen

admin: May be taken with or without food
Screen for G6PD deficiency before starting and treat severe anemia first
In leprosy, always combine with one or more other anti-leprosy drugs to limit resistance
Warn patients to report sore throat, fever, pallor, purpura or jaundice immediately
moa: Dapsone is bacteriostatic and bactericidal against Mycobacterium leprae by inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folate synthesis (similar to sulfonamides). In dermatitis herpetiformis and other neutrophilic dermatoses, its anti-inflammatory effect is attributed to suppression of neutrophil myeloperoxidase, chemotaxis and reactive-oxygen production rather than its antibacterial action.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to dapsone or its derivatives
relative: Methemoglobin reductase deficiency or hemoglobin M

preg: Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed; dapsone crosses the placenta and can cause hemolysis. In leprosy and dermatitis herpetiformis the benefit may justify use, with folic acid supplementation and monitoring.
lact: Dapsone is excreted in breast milk and can cause hemolytic anemia in the infant, particularly if the infant is G6PD-deficient. Weigh benefit against risk; monitor the infant.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; no specific dosing schedule is given - monitor for toxicity.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; monitor liver function tests as dapsone can cause hepatitis and cholestatic jaundice.

major: Folic acid antagonists e.g. pyrimethamine, methotrexate (increased hematologic toxicity, agranulocytosis)
moderate: Rifampin (lowers dapsone levels by inducing metabolism)
Trimethoprim (mutually increased levels; additive hematologic toxicity)
minor: Activated charcoal (reduces enterohepatic recirculation - used therapeutically in overdose)
interactions.diagnostics: Causes dose-related rise in methemoglobin; lowers hemoglobin and raises reticulocytes; may raise bilirubin/LFTs

serious: Aplastic anemia and other blood dyscrasias (can be fatal)
Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome / DRESS (fever, rash, hepatitis, eosinophilia)
rare: Severe cutaneous reactions including exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis

monitoring: Complete blood count weekly for the first month, monthly for 6 months, then semi-annually
Methemoglobin level if cyanosis or dyspnea
Signs of hypersensitivity (rash, fever) and peripheral neuropathy
counsel: Report sore throat, fever, pallor, unusual bruising/bleeding, or yellowing of eyes/skin right away - these may signal serious blood or liver problems
Bluish discoloration of lips/skin (methemoglobinemia) needs medical attention
Do not stop leprosy treatment early; take it with the other prescribed drugs
A rash with fever in the first weeks can be a dangerous hypersensitivity reaction - seek care immediately
pk: Anti-inflammatory benefit in dermatitis herpetiformis often within days (rapid reduction in pruritus)
Plasma peak ~2-8 hours after oral dose
Long; once-daily dosing; undergoes enterohepatic recirculation
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from light
pearls: Always screen for G6PD deficiency before starting - dapsone causes dose-dependent hemolysis, severe in G6PD deficiency
Blood dyscrasias (agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia) can be fatal: CBC weekly x1 month, monthly x6 months, then semi-annually
Dapsone hypersensitivity (DRESS) syndrome - fever, rash, hepatitis, eosinophilia - is a key delayed, potentially fatal reaction
Methemoglobinemia is treated with methylene blue (avoid methylene blue in G6PD deficiency); acetylation rate influences levels
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule - do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Overdose causes severe methemoglobinemia (cyanosis, dyspnea), hemolysis, nausea, vomiting and CNS excitation/depression. Treat with methylene blue for significant methemoglobinemia (contraindicated in G6PD deficiency - use exchange transfusion/oxygen instead), activated charcoal (interrupts enterohepatic recirculation, repeated doses), and supportive care.
